item.title: Diagnostic and sex effects on frontostriatal brain wiring structural organization in early psychosis affective subjects compared to healthy controls.
item.author: Levitt JJ, Zhang F, Vangel M, Nestor PG, Rathi Y, Cetin-Karayumak S, Kubicki M, Pasternak O, Coleman MJ, Lewandowski KE, Holt DJ, Keshavan M, Bouix S, Öngür D, Breier A, Shenton ME, O'Donnell LJ.
item.description:
Background Brain connectivity abnormalities may underlie affective psychosis which may be influenced by sex. Using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography, we assessed frontostriatal brain wiring connectivity patterns in 46 early psychosis affective and 56 healthy control young adult, male and female participants. Methods We collected harmonized whole brain tractography dMRI data from three sites and applied our novel fiber clustering methodology to identify 17 white matter fiber clusters connecting the frontal cortex and caudate per hemisphere in each group. By comparing cortical and caudate inter-cluster endpoint distances between groups, we assessed their patterns of frontostriatal connectivity. item.title: Cannabinoid receptor type 1 availability in individuals with a history of childhood trauma: a positron emission tomography study.
item.author: Mohammad Aghaei A, Pittman B, Korem N, Potenza MN, D'Souza DC, Hillmer AT, Ranganathan M, Harpaz-Rotem I, Bassir Nia A.
item.description:
Early life adversity has a lasting impact on the endocannabinoid (eCB) system based on animal models. However, the impact of early life adversity, such as childhood trauma (CT), on the eCB system has not been thoroughly studied. We assessed the availability of cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1R) in individuals with CT compared to healthy controls without CT (HCs). Cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1R) availability was compared in adults with CT (N = 22) and age- and sex-matched HCs (n = 22), using positron emission tomography (PET) imaging with the CB1R-specific radiotracer [11C]OMAR. Using linear models, the effect of the group was assessed on global and trauma-relevant brain regions (amygdala, hippocampus, and frontal cortex). item.title: State-dependent effects of rTMS on cognitive function in bipolar II disorder: A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
item.author: Wang M, Chen Q, Tang E, Qi S, Tang R, Zhang J, Zhou H, Du L, Chen H, Hu S.
item.description:
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a promising neuromodulatory approach for cognitive improvement in psychiatric disorders. However, whether concurrent cognitive engagement enhances rTMS-related effects remains unclear. In this exploratory, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled 2 × 2 factorial trial, 96 euthymic patients with bipolar II disorder and subjective cognitive impairment were assigned to active or sham 10-Hz rTMS combined with either a complex or simple cognitive task. Stimulation targeted the left inferior parietal lobule (IPL) using robot-assisted neuronavigation and was delivered in 10 sessions over 5 consecutive days. The main outcomes included changes in working memory capacity and precision, subjective cognitive performance (Perceived Deficits Questionnaire, PDQ), and resting-state fMRI connectivity within hippocampal and IPL networks. item.title: Genotype and phenotype analyses of 689 individuals with PCDH19-clustering epilepsy.
item.author: Grasso KM, Corbett MA, Scheffer IE, Gecz J.
item.description:
PCDH19-clustering epilepsy (PCDH19-CE) is an infantile-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by clusters of seizures, typically triggered by fever. PCDH19-CE follows an unusual X-linked inheritance pattern whereby heterozygous females, and males with X-chromosome disomy or pathogenic postzygotic mosaic PCDH19 variants, are affected, while hemizygous males are spared. We aggregate published PCDH19 variants and their corresponding PCDH19-CE phenotypes to analyse phenotype-genotype correlations. Data extracted from 110 publications identified 689/735 (94%) individuals with PCDH19 variants and the typical PCDH19-CE phenotype. Three hundred seventy-three unique PCDH19 variants were identified; 195 were not recorded in ClinVar. item.title: A Crh-defined insular cortex-brainstem-thalamic circuit regulates anxiety-related behavioral states.
item.author: An ZY, Liu MZ, Yuan JY, Song MY, Yang XM, He Y, Mu D.
item.description:
Anxiety disorders are among the most prevalent and debilitating psychiatric conditions, yet the neural circuits underlying anxiety-related states remain incompletely understood. Here we identify a cortical-brainstem-thalamic pathway in which Crh-expressing neurons in the anterior and middle insular cortex (a/mIC) engage the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), which in turn recruits the posterior paraventricular thalamic nucleus (pPVT) to contribute to anxiety-related behavior. Single-cell calcium imaging reveals that the predator odorant 2-methyl-2-thiazoline (2-MT) and footshock recruit partially overlapping populations of PBN-projecting a/mIC neurons; neurons activated by both stimuli exhibit increased activity during open-arm approach in the elevated plus maze. item.title: Identification of fluid endocannabinoid and sphingolipid biomarkers in schizophrenia. A machine learning approach toward clinical value.
item.author: Hoffmann AE, Allwright M, Guennewig B, Rohleder C, Jieu B, Koethe D, Dammann I, Del Castillo AA, Mueller JK, Enning F, Shepherd CE, Couttas TA, Leweke FM.
item.description:
Schizophrenia (SCZ) diagnosis relies on subjective clinical evaluation, with symptoms often overlapping between psychiatric conditions, hindering early intervention, and creating an urgent need for objective, accessible biomarkers. Lipids, especially endocannabinoid system (ECS) and sphingolipid metabolism members, are promising candidates given their implication in SCZ pathogenesis and measurability in accessible biofluids, with minimally invasive procedures. Our study conducted the first comprehensive crossover of endocannabinoids (eCBs) and sphingolipids in matched cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum samples from antipsychotic-naïve SCZ patients (SCZ naïve , n = 49), antipsychotic-treated patients (SCZ treat , n = 56), and healthy volunteers (HVs, n = 51). item.title: Mitochondrial complex IV disruption is a detrimental pathology conferring ssusceptibility to alzheimer's disease.
item.author: Tian J, Jia K, Chen Y, Wang T, Guo L, Swerdlow RH, Du H.
item.description:
Mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) is an integral part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and plays a pivotal role in maintaining mitochondrial function. In contrast to the long-standing recognition of its dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD), the exact role of CIV deficit in the pathogenesis of this neurodegenerative disorder remains poorly defined. In this study, by incorporating clinical resources, mouse- and human-based models of AD risk, and a genetic approach to bypass defective CIV via the ectopic expression of alternative oxidase (AOX), we examined whether CIV deficits are a pathogenic driver of or a beneficial adaptation to AD-associated pathologies. Our results showed a clinicopathological association between neuronal CIV dysfunction and pathological characteristics of AD. item.title: Polygenic dissection of suicidal thoughts and behaviours in high-risk mood-disorder cohorts.
item.author: Ceja Z, García-Marín LM, Hickie IB, Martin NG, Medland SE, Rentería ME, Edwards AC.
item.description:
Suicidal thoughts and behaviours (STB) span ideation (SI), attempt (SA), and death (SD), yet the factors distinguishing ideation from attempt remain poorly understood. Genome-wide studies suggest shared yet partially distinct genetic liabilities. However, few analyses have tested the differential contributions of SI-, SA-, and SD-related genetic liability across STB phenotypes, particularly in high-risk mood-disorder populations. We analysed up to 17,622 participants from the Australian Genetics of Depression Study and the Australian Genetics of Bipolar Disorder study, jointly modelling polygenic scores (PGS) for SI, SA, and SD across mutually exclusive STB phenotypes using multinomial regression, alongside dimensional outcomes, age of onset, and the ideation-to-attempt transition. item.title: Tryptophan metabolism within the gut-brain axis in depression: mechanisms, association with heterogeneity, and therapeutic opportunities.
item.author: Qin Z, Lei T, Yi T, Zhang S, Tang Y, Xiang Y, Zhou Z, Mei Z, Qiu F, Zhang X.
item.description:
Depression is a highly heterogeneous psychiatric disorder, characterized by substantial variability in clinical manifestations, treatment responses, and disease progression, thereby posing significant challenges to precision diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence indicates that dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, mediated through dynamic crosstalk with the gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis (GBA), plays a pivotal role in both the pathophysiology and biological heterogeneity of depression. In this review, we delineate the contributions of the three principal tryptophan metabolic pathways-the kynurenine, serotonin, and microbial indole pathways-in modulating neuroimmune signaling, neurotransmitter function, and gut-brain communication. item.title: Multivariate genome-wide association study of post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use, and alcohol use disorders.
item.author: Barr PB, Bountress K, Chatzinakos C, Hart JE, Neale ZE, Sheerin C, Johnson E, Atkinson EG, Nievergelt CM, Maihofer AX, Powers A, Porjesz B, Agrawal A, Edenberg HJ, Gelernter J, Koenen KC, PTSD workgroup of the Psychiatric Genomic Consortium (PGC-PTSD), Amstadter AB, Meyers JL.
item.description:
Alcohol use disorder (AUD) commonly co-occurs with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Comorbid PTSD and AUD is associated with poorer outcomes including worse treatment prognosis and significant physical health consequences. Both PTSD and AUD are polygenic in nature and genetically overlap. Previous work showed negative or non-significant associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption but positive genetic associations between PTSD and AUD. This work highlights the need for more nuanced examination of the similarities and distinctions in the associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption versus AUD. We leveraged the latest large-scale GWAS data to perform a multivariate GWAS of alcohol consumption (ALCC), problematic alcohol use (ALCP), and PTSD using GenomicSEM.
